title: What Are the Westminster Standards?
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 1
description: An introduction to the Westminster Assembly and the three documents it produced — the Confession of Faith, the Larger Catechism, and the Shorter Catechism — their historical context, purpose, and enduring significance.
reviewQuestions: When and where was the Westminster Assembly convened, and what was its purpose?
What are the three primary documents that make up the Westminster Standards?
What is the first question and answer of the Westminster Shorter Catechism?
activity: Create a timeline poster of the Westminster Assembly with key dates, figures, and historical context of the English Civil War.

title: The Doctrine of Scripture
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 2
description: Explore Chapter 1 of the Westminster Confession — the necessity, authority, sufficiency, and clarity of Holy Scripture. Understand why the doctrine of Scripture is the logical starting point for all theology.
reviewQuestions: Why does the Westminster Confession begin with the doctrine of Scripture?
What is the ultimate basis for the authority of Scripture according to the Confession?
What does the Confession mean by the 'sufficiency' and 'clarity' of Scripture?
activity: Read Chapter 1 of the Westminster Confession and create a one-page summary chart covering Necessity, Canon, Authority, Sufficiency, Clarity, and Interpretation of Scripture.

title: The Doctrine of God — His Being and Attributes
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 3
description: Ascend to the highest subject of human thought — the doctrine of God. Study the Shorter Catechism's magnificent answer to 'What is God?' and explore each divine attribute and the doctrine of the Trinity.
reviewQuestions: Recite the Shorter Catechism's answer to 'What is God?' and explain each quality: Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable.
What are the seven attributes listed in the Catechism's answer and what does each mean?
What does the Westminster Confession teach about the Trinity?
activity: Create an 'Attributes of God' reference card with definitions, Bible verses, and corresponding hymns or psalms for each attribute.

title: God's Eternal Decrees and Providence
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 4
description: Explore the awe-inspiring doctrines of God's eternal decrees and providential governance — how God has ordained whatsoever comes to pass and governs all things from the greatest to the least.
reviewQuestions: What does the Confession mean when it says God 'ordained whatsoever comes to pass'? How does this relate to human responsibility?
What is the difference between God's eternal decrees and His providence?
How does the Confession address the relationship between God's sovereignty and evil?
activity: Write a two-paragraph essay comparing God's sovereignty with human responsibility, using quotations from the Confession and supporting Scripture passages.

title: Creation, the Fall, and the Covenant of Grace
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 5
description: Trace the great narrative arc of Scripture — from the glory of creation through the tragedy of the fall to the hope of the covenant of grace. Understand the doctrines of the image of God, original sin, and redemption.
reviewQuestions: What does the Westminster Confession teach about the creation of humanity and the image of God?
What was the covenant of works, and what happened when Adam broke it?
What is the covenant of grace and how does it differ from the covenant of works?
activity: Create a three-panel visual presentation of Creation, Fall, and Redemption with Scripture references, Confession quotations, and personal reflections.

title: The Person and Work of Christ
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 6
description: Come to the heart of the Christian faith — the person and work of Jesus Christ. Study His two natures, three offices (Prophet, Priest, King), and the doctrine of penal substitutionary atonement.
reviewQuestions: What does the Shorter Catechism teach about the two natures of Christ?
Explain Christ's three offices — Prophet, Priest, and King — and how each contributes to salvation.
What is penal substitutionary atonement and how does the Confession describe it?
activity: Create a study sheet on Christ's three offices with definitions, Scripture passages, and explanations of how each office is fulfilled in both humiliation and exaltation.

title: The Application of Redemption
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 7
description: Explore how Christ's salvation is applied to individual believers through the doctrines of effectual calling, justification, and adoption — the Trinitarian work of bringing sinners into the family of God.
reviewQuestions: What is effectual calling and how does it differ from a general invitation to believe?
Explain the two aspects of justification — pardon and imputed righteousness.
What is adoption, and what privileges does it bring?
activity: Create a flowchart showing the order of salvation — effectual calling, faith, repentance, justification, and adoption — with descriptions and Scripture verses for each step.

title: Sanctification and Perseverance
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 8
description: Study the lifelong process of sanctification — growing in holiness through the war between flesh and Spirit — and the comforting doctrine that true believers will persevere to the end by God's sustaining grace.
reviewQuestions: What is sanctification and how does it differ from justification?
What does the Confession mean by the 'continual and irreconcilable war' between flesh and Spirit?
What does the doctrine of perseverance teach, and why is it comforting?
activity: Design a two-column chart titled 'Mortification and Vivification' listing sins to put to death and virtues to put on, with Scripture references and a personal prayer for growth.

title: The Church, Sacraments, and Means of Grace
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 9
description: Examine the Westminster teaching on the visible and invisible church, the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, and the ordinary means of grace — Word, sacrament, and prayer — through which God sustains His people.
reviewQuestions: What is the difference between the visible and invisible church?
What are the three 'outward and ordinary means' of grace, and why are they called 'ordinary'?
How does the Confession understand the Lord's Supper?
activity: Create a 'Means of Grace' study guide with three sections — Word, Sacraments, and Prayer — including summaries, catechism questions, and Scripture passages for each.

title: The Last Things — Death, Judgment, and Eternity
subtitle: Westminster Standards — Lesson 10
description: Conclude the Westminster Standards unit with the doctrine of the last things — the intermediate state, the bodily resurrection, the final judgment, and the eternal states of glory and condemnation.
reviewQuestions: What happens to believers at death? What is the 'intermediate state'?
What is the doctrine of the bodily resurrection and why does it matter?
What is the purpose of the final judgment?
activity: Write a one-page essay titled 'The Christian Hope' summarizing what the Westminster Standards teach about death, resurrection, judgment, and eternity, with direct quotations and Scripture references.

title: What Is Apologetics and Why Does It Matter?
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 11
description: Begin the study of Christian apologetics — the art and discipline of defending the faith. Learn what apologetics means, why it matters for young Christians, and the three main approaches to defending the faith.
reviewQuestions: What does the word 'apologetics' mean and where does it come from in Scripture?
Why does apologetics matter for young Christians? Give at least three reasons.
What are the three main approaches to apologetics?
activity: Read 1 Peter 3:15-16 and write a paraphrase in your own words. Then list three questions about Christianity you have heard or asked, to revisit at the end of the unit.

title: Does God Exist? Arguments from Creation
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 12
description: Examine the foundational question of apologetics — Does God exist? — through three powerful arguments: the Cosmological Argument, the Teleological Argument, and the Moral Argument.
reviewQuestions: Explain the Cosmological Argument in your own words.
What is the Teleological Argument and how does fine-tuning point to a Designer?
How does the Moral Argument work?
activity: Choose one argument for God's existence and write a two-paragraph summary explaining it to an imaginary friend who does not believe in God. Practice responding to one objection.

title: Can We Trust the Bible?
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 13
description: Examine the evidence for the reliability of the Bible from three angles: manuscript evidence, archaeological confirmation, and internal consistency including fulfilled prophecy.
reviewQuestions: How does the manuscript evidence for the New Testament compare to other ancient documents?
Give two examples of archaeological discoveries that have confirmed the Bible's accuracy.
How does the internal consistency of the Bible point to divine inspiration?
activity: Create a three-column comparison chart comparing the manuscript evidence for the New Testament with other ancient texts like Homer's Iliad and Plato's works.

title: The Resurrection of Jesus — The Heart of the Evidence
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 14
description: Examine the single most important event in the defense of the Christian faith — the bodily resurrection of Jesus. Study five historical facts that form the evidential foundation and refute alternative explanations.
reviewQuestions: What are the five historical facts that form the evidential foundation for the resurrection?
Why is the testimony of women as first witnesses significant for historicity?
Choose one alternative explanation for the resurrection and explain why it fails.
activity: Prepare a five-minute oral presentation defending the resurrection of Jesus using the five facts discussed in the lesson. Practice with a family member who asks questions.

title: The Problem of Evil and Suffering
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 15
description: Confront the most emotionally powerful objection to Christianity — the problem of evil — and discover the Christian resources for addressing it: free will, the fall, the cross, and future glory.
reviewQuestions: State the logical problem of evil in your own words. Why is the assumption behind it unjustified?
How do the doctrines of free will, the fall, and redemption help address the problem of evil?
Why might the problem of evil be a greater difficulty for atheism than for Christianity?
activity: Write a compassionate letter to an imaginary friend struggling with the problem of evil after a personal tragedy, sharing Christian resources discussed in the lesson.

title: Science and the Christian Faith
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 16
description: Dismantle the myth that science and Christianity are at war. Discover how the Christian worldview provided the intellectual foundation for modern science and how faith and reason work together.
reviewQuestions: How did the Christian worldview provide the intellectual foundation for the rise of modern science?
Name three major scientists who were devout Christians and explain how their faith related to their work.
What is the difference between science and scientism?
activity: Research one of the Christian scientists mentioned in the lesson. Write a one-page biographical sketch including scientific contributions, Christian faith, and a direct quotation about God.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 17
description: Address the culturally sensitive question of religious exclusivity. Examine the biblical basis for Christ's unique claim, compare the core teachings of major world religions, and learn to share this truth with grace.
reviewQuestions: What did Jesus claim about Himself in John 14:6 and why is this significant?
Why can't all religions be 'basically the same'? Give two examples of fundamental contradictions.
How can Christians communicate the exclusivity of Christ without being arrogant?
activity: Create a comparison chart of Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism on three key topics: the nature of God, the human problem, and the solution. Identify contradictions.

title: Answering Moral Objections to Christianity
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 18
description: Address three common moral objections: that the Bible endorses violence, that Christians are hypocrites, and that religion has done more harm than good. Learn to respond with honesty and grace.
reviewQuestions: How should Christians understand the violence in the Old Testament?
How should Christians respond to the charge of hypocrisy?
Is the claim that 'religion has done more harm than good' historically accurate?
activity: Choose one of the three moral objections and write a one-page response to someone who has raised it. Acknowledge legitimate concerns while providing a thoughtful Christian answer.

title: The Christian Worldview — Making Sense of Everything
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 19
description: Step back to see the big picture: how the Christian worldview answers the four great questions of life — origin, problem, solution, and destiny — and how it compares to secular naturalism.
reviewQuestions: What is a worldview, and why does everyone have one?
How does the Christian worldview answer the four big questions differently from secular naturalism?
Why does secular naturalism struggle to provide a foundation for meaning, morality, and hope?
activity: Create a four-quadrant poster comparing the Christian worldview and secular naturalism on origin, problem, solution, and destiny. Write a paragraph explaining which you find more coherent.

title: Sharing Your Faith with Confidence and Grace
subtitle: Apologetics for Young Christians — Lesson 20
description: Put everything together in this capstone lesson. Learn five principles for sharing and defending your faith in real conversations — listening, honesty, gospel focus, embodied witness, and trust in the Holy Spirit.
reviewQuestions: What are the five principles of effective apologetics discussed in this lesson?
Why is listening more important than speaking in apologetic conversations?
What is the relationship between apologetics and the gospel?
activity: Practice a role-play conversation with a family member playing a respectful non-Christian who raises one objection studied in this unit. Apply all five principles. Discuss what went well and what could improve.
